report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is supported for *prescription, purified cannabidiol added to existing antiseizure medicines* in children (and some young adults) with drug-resistant Dravet syndrome. It should not be generalized to over-the-counter CBD products, which were not tested.

The strongest evidence is a 120-patient, randomized, double-blind trial: over 14 weeks, convulsive-seizure frequency fell by a median 39% with cannabidiol (20 mg/kg/day) versus 13% with placebo. At least a 50% reduction occurred in 43% versus 27%, respectively.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618

A subsequent randomized dose-ranging trial also found clinically meaningful reductions with add-on cannabidiol 10 or 20 mg/kg/day; the 10-mg/kg dose had better tolerability.  
https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458

A systematic review/meta-analysis of placebo-controlled trials likewise evaluated adjunctive CBD as effective, supporting that this is not based on a single trial.  
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-020-00708-6

**Important qualifications:** benefits are incomplete—most participants did not become seizure-free—and trials were relatively short and involved severely treatment-resistant patients. Adverse effects were more frequent than with placebo, including diarrhea, reduced appetite, sleepiness/fatigue, vomiting, and liver-enzyme elevations; interaction/monitoring issues matter particularly with valproate and clobazam. The FDA label documents the controlled-trial basis and safety monitoring requirements.  
https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2018/210365lbl.pdf
